source.title: The Low-Resource Double Bind: An Empirical Study of Pruning for Low-Resource Machine Translation
source.authors: Orevaoghene Ahia; Julia Kreutzer; Sara Hooker

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices and tables.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how magnitude pruning affects in-domain and out-of-distribution translation quality in low-resource machine translation, a new setting for the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports separate pruning and training-regime results, human ratings, sentence-typicality results, and distribution-shift evaluations. Cited results about memorization from other work are not extracted as this study's results. OOD results are recorded as findings about the claim's subject, but do not test the versions' in-distribution generalization claims.
record.test_reason: The study tests magnitude pruning in machine translation, which none of V1–V8 names. Changing weight sparsity does not test widening beyond interpolation, and sentence typicality does not identify memorized examples by inclusion influence or test their removal. Citing V8's source and discussing memorization do not make this a test of V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that pruning preserves much translation quality, disproportionately reduces fitting of infrequent patterns, and improves OOD robustness under limited training data. Add that the relative OOD advantage disappears with Full German training and that human ratings remain similar at 90% sparsity. Reduced memorization is their interpretation of typicality and transfer results, rather than an influence-based measurement or example-removal experiment.
record.recipe_differences: Magnitude pruning of transformer NMT models trained on natural translation data; evaluates BLEU, human ratings, sentence-typicality groups, and domain-shift performance. Does not use the original claim versions' image-classification, optimizer, batch, dropout, sharpness, or example-removal protocols.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with sparsity level, training-data regime, test-set construction, language, and domain shift.

fits_no_version.finding: At 50%–80% sparsity, translation BLEU remains close to dense performance; extreme sparsity produces larger losses. Under Limited training, the authors report an OOD advantage around 70%–95% sparsity. The relative advantage disappears with Full German training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Magnitude pruning's effect on translation generalization depends on sparsity, training-data size, and evaluation distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: Dense German training BLEU exceeds sparse BLEU in every typicality group, especially low typicality: 62.04 versus 24.93. On Random test sentences, sparse BLEU is slightly higher only in the low-typicality group, 23.08 versus 22.35; dense scores higher in every Global test group.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pruning reduces fitting of atypical training sentences, while held-out effects vary by sentence typicality and test-set construction.

fits_no_version.finding: Human ratings of differing dense and 90%-sparse translations are similar overall, with German ratings modestly favoring dense outputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pruning to 90% sparsity can preserve average human-rated translation quality in the tested low-resource settings.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: No random-label or chance-level test; no uncertainty estimates reported for the extracted result tables; several distribution-shift results are shown only in figures without exact values in the supplied text; conclusions are limited to translation models, languages, corpora, and training settings studied.
record.rows_left_out: No required rows left out. Figure-level per-corpus distribution-shift comparisons are not separately extracted because the supplied text provides no exact per-corpus values and the plots are not transcribed; the explicit aggregate textual result is recorded in R13–R16.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the paired natural-label versus random-label held-out comparison.
Width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error; pruning is a different intervention.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning; the study uses adafactor without an optimizer comparison.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout interventions; dropout is held at 0.1 rather than compared.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, generalization-gap rankings, and competing measures.
Influence-based identification and removal of memorized training examples, retraining, and comparison with random removal.

record.verdict_notes: T6 applies relative to these eight versions, despite the study conducting its own generalization experiments. No version-specific verdict is warranted. The absence of a chance baseline is not the central exclusion: the named interventions and comparisons are missing. Table 2's layout caused the substantive R9 extraction error.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or natural-label versus random-label held-out comparison.
No width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-model comparison.
No sharpness or other generalization-measure comparison.
No removal of memorized training examples followed by retraining.
